newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police head of violence at protest rally.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police head of violence at protest rally.

text.p: Albanian police and international troops combined on Friday to prevent a recurrence of violence that threatened to derail crucial elections as votes were still being counted five days after the first round of polling.

A heavy police presence prevented about 200 royalists from marching on the central electoral commission as they did on Thursday, when a protest rally erupted into shooting outside the building. One man was killed and several were injured.

The royalist marchers, joined by Albania's self-proclaimed king, Leka I, were protesting against alleged rigging of a referendum also held last Sunday in which Albanians voted by nearly two to one against restoring the monarchy, banished when Italy invaded in 1939.
The protesters accuse the opposition Socialists, who according to preliminary results are heading for a sweeping victory in the two-round general elections, of rigging the referendum.

The elections were called earlier this year to end violence and anarchy in the country following the collapse of shady pyramid savings schemes. The crumbling schemes left thousands of families bankrupted.

Despite fierce prodding by increasingly impatient international monitors overseeing the election, officials were unable to give a breakdown of seats won in last Sunday's first round of voting by late afternoon on Friday.

Election officials did manage to give monitors from the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) a list of more than 30 districts where run-off polls will be held this Sunday, enabling ballot papers to be printed in time.

According to preliminary results the Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists who ran the country with an iron grip for four decades, had won 49 seats compared to just eight for the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha.
Berisha has already conceded defeat and pledged to honour a campaign promise to step down once the final tally confirms the Democrats have lost.
The royalist rally took place in Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square, despite warnings by police that unauthorised demonstrations were banned under emergency regulations in force since March.

Unlike Thursday's rally attended by about 500 people in the square, a strong presence of police, with automatic weapons, flak jackets and dogs, prevented protesters from marching to the electoral commission some 600 metres (yards) away.

Troops from a multinational force sent to Albania in April to help deliver humanitarian aid and prepare the elections were also much in evidence, cruising the streets around the electoral commission in jeeps and armoured cars.

Leka arrived at the rally with a police escort, but unlike the previous day when he was dressed in battle fatigues with two pistols in his belt, he wore a safari suit. Neither he or his bodyguards were armed.
Earlier rival political parties traded charges of responsibility for Thursday's violence.

Officials of Berisha's defeated Democrats and royalists said police fired at unarmed protesters. But a top electoral official inside said it was the protesters who shot first. Witnesses said most firing seemed to be into the air.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright sent a letter to Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino expressing satisfaction that the first round of elections had been completed.

Saying this was only the first step in rebuilding the shattered country, she added: "To ensure continued progress, it will be necessary for all parties in Albania to maintain their commitment to the spirit of national reconciliation."
"For its part, the United States will remain fully engaged in Albania and will continue to work through the OSCE to see that the reconstruction of your country continues to move forward."
